function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run `git` commands or actually clone a repository from GitHub, so I can’t inspect the real contents of `nodejs-welcome`.  
What I *can* do is give you ready‑to‑drop templates for the three artifacts you asked for:

| Artifact | What it does | Where to put it |
|----------|--------------|-----------------|
| **Dockerfile** | Builds a lightweight image that runs your Node.js app. | In the root of the repo (or wherever your source lives). |
| **Kubernetes YAML** | Deploys two replicas behind a ClusterIP service. | In a `k8s/` folder (you can change the location later). |
| **GitHub Actions workflow** | Builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub whenever you push to `main`. | `.github/workflows/build.yml` |

Below are the exact files you can copy into your repo. Once you’ve added them, just run the usual `git add`, `git commit`, and `git push`.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this one?**  
> - `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> - `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> - Exposes port 3000 – adjust if your app uses another port.  

If your repo already contains a Dockerfile, replace it with the snippet above or merge the relevant parts.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to tweak it**  
> - Change `replicas` if you want more or fewer pods.  
> - Update `image:` to point at the correct registry/tag.  
> - If you need external access, switch `type: ClusterIP` → `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/build.yml`)

```yaml
name: Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        push: true
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> 1. Create a Docker Hub account.  
> 2. Add two repository secrets to your GitHub repo:  
>    - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub login.  
>    - `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a personal access token with “write” permissions.  

Once those secrets exist, the workflow will automatically build the image and push it to Docker Hub whenever you push to `main`.

---

## 4️⃣ Adding, Committing, Pushing

```bash
# From the root of the cloned repo
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI pipeline"
git push origin main
```

That’s all you need to get the repo set up for containerization, Kubernetes deployment, and continuous integration. Happy coding!
